title: skillgrade
description: Unit tests for agent skills — run assertions against agent skill outputs the same way you'd test code
why: Solves the 'how do I know my agent skill actually works' problem with a familiar test-runner interface. From Minko Gechev (Angular team). 480 stars in ~3 months.
author: @mgechev

title: agent-skills-eval
description: Test runner for agentskills.io-style skills with YAML-based scenarios and LLM judges
why: 508 stars in 2 weeks. The agentskills.io spec is getting traction and this gives it a proper eval framework. TypeScript, works with OpenAI-compatible APIs.
author: @darkrishabh

title: eval-view
description: Regression testing for AI agents — snapshot behavior, diff tool calls, catch regressions in CI
why: Works with LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI, Anthropic. The snapshot-diff approach is exactly what agent teams need but few build. Python/pytest-based.
author: @hidai25

title: agent-belt
description: Reproducible evaluation for AI coding agents — multi-turn scenarios, rich assertions, multi-judge consensus
why: From JFrog's engineering team. Runs eval scenarios against Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, or any agent you plug in. Open source, CLI-based. Fills the 'how do I test my coding agent doesn't break' gap.
author: @jfrog

title: contrabass
description: Project-level orchestrator for AI coding agents — Go + Charm TUI implementation of OpenAI's Symphony SPEC.md
why: First real implementation of the Symphony spec. Go binary, TUI interface, coordinates Codex/Claude Code agents. 151 stars, actively maintained. The 'one orchestrator, many coding CLIs' pattern is where agent infra is heading.
author: @junhoyeo

title: OpenAI Symphony SPEC.md
description: OpenAI open-sourced Symphony, a SPEC.md for autonomous coding agent orchestration
why: Defines a standard for how coding agents should be orchestrated — issue intake, agent spawning, artifact management. Already spawning implementations (contrabass, symphony forks). This is the 'docker-compose for coding agents' moment.
author: @OpenAI

title: TraceFix
description: Uses TLA+ counterexamples to repair multi-agent LLM coordination protocols before deployment
why: Formal methods applied to agent coordination. Instead of testing protocols after they fail, TLA+ finds violations upfront and generates repairs. CAISconf 2026 paper by Rutgers team.
author: @jortiz81

title: Raindrop Workshop
description: Local debugger for AI agents — live streamed traces of every token, tool call, and decision with self-healing eval loops
why: Solves the 'agent debugging is blind' problem. You can watch agents think in real time, and Claude Code reads the traces, writes evals, and fixes bugs autonomously. MIT license, 665 stars in 18 days. Works with every major SDK and coding agent.
author: @raindrop_ai

title: claude-mem
description: Persistent context across sessions for coding agents — captures session activity, compresses with AI, injects into future sessions
why: Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot. 76k stars, v13.2, active commits. Solves the real problem of agents starting from zero every session. SQLite + ChromaDB + embeddings under the hood.
author: @thedotmack

title: 12-Factor Agents
description: Engineering principles for building production-grade LLM-powered software — agents as software with LLM steps, not prompt loops
why: 21k stars. The core insight: agents are software with LLM calls placed strategically, not 'prompt + tools + loop'. Own your prompts, typed tools, human-in-the-loop as first-class, stateless reducer pattern. This is the production playbook most agent projects lack.
author: @humanlayer

title: Google Antigravity 2.0
description: Google's multi-agent orchestration platform — standalone desktop app, CLI, SDK, voice. Gemini 3.5 Flash runs 12x faster within the framework
why: Announced at Google I/O 2026. Already has ecosystem: opencode-antigravity-auth (10k stars), VS Code extensions, skill collections. The 'one platform to command agent teams' pattern consolidating. Early preview, globally available.
author: @Google

title: Context7
description: Up-to-date code documentation delivered to LLMs and code editors via MCP — solves the stale-doc problem for coding agents
why: 55k stars, MIT. The real issue: every coding agent guesses APIs from training data that's months old. Context7 injects fresh docs at query time. Works as MCP server, integrates with Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex. Built by Upstash. The 'documentation as context' pattern is a missing infra layer for agent reliability.
author: @upstash

title: Chrome DevTools MCP
description: Official Chrome DevTools exposed as MCP server — lets coding agents inspect, debug, and profile web apps directly
why: 40k stars, Apache 2.0, official Google project. The first serious bridge between browser debugging and agent workflows. Agents can now read console errors, inspect DOM, profile performance, and set breakpoints — all through structured tool calls instead of screenshot guessing. Changes how agents debug frontend code.
author: @ChromeDevTools

title: Lapdog (Datadog)
description: Local agent tracer — traces reasoning and tool calls from Codex, Claude Code, and Pi in real time, no account required
why: Datadog shipped a free local tool that shows what agents actually do. 70 likes in hours. Fills a real gap: most agent debugging is reading terminal output blind. Runs fully local, zero infra. The 'observability for agents' layer is barely starting and this is the first usable tool from a major vendor.
author: @astuyve

title: Retrieval Routing: vector + GraphRAG + PageIndex
description: Production pattern: route queries across vector RAG, GraphRAG, and PageIndex based on query type using a lightweight classifier before retrieval
why: The insight: most teams pick one retrieval strategy and force everything through it. Wrong retrieval produces wrong answers that compound into agent failures. A small LLM classifier in front of the retrieval layer costs less than one bad retrieval. Vector for factual lookup, GraphRAG for multi-hop relational, PageIndex for long structured docs. FinanceBench: vector scores 50%, PageIndex scores 98.7%.
author: @NullS0S

title: Cloudflare + Claude Managed Agents isolated execution
description: Cloudflare integrates with Anthropic's Claude Managed Agents to provide isolated sandboxed execution environments for autonomous code delivery at edge scale
why: 363 likes, 35k views. The 'isolated agent runtime' pattern is consolidating fast — Cloudflare, Vercel, and Google all shipped sandbox integrations in the same week. This is the missing infra layer for production agents: bounded blast radius, controlled access to private backends, custom runtimes. The pattern: cloud providers own the sandbox, model providers own the agent runtime.
author: @Cloudflare

title: Ruflo
description: Agent orchestration platform for Claude — deploy multi-agent workflows with a visual builder and structured output routing
why: 53k stars. First major orchestration platform built specifically for the Claude ecosystem. The 'single agent framework, many providers' era is giving way to framework-specific orchestration layers. TypeScript, visual workflow builder, supports Claude Code and OpenClaw natively.
author: @ruvnet

title: MassGen
description: Open-source multi-agent scaling system with TUI — agents work in parallel, vote on best solutions via consensus, with checklist-gated quality rounds
why: 1034 stars. The consensus voting mechanism is genuinely different from other orchestrators. Agents collaborate, vote to converge, and self-evaluate with evolving criteria. Worktree isolation per agent, MCP tool support, checkpoint safety as standalone MCP server. Python/TUI. Fills the "how do multiple agents agree on an answer" gap.
author: @massgen_ai

title: pentest-ai
description: Offensive security MCP server — wraps 205 pentesting tools and 17 specialist agents behind a single MCP interface
why: 268 stars, MIT license. The first serious attempt to put offensive security behind MCP. 205 tools (nmap, exploitation, OSINT) accessible to any MCP client. Shows MCP reaching beyond dev tools into security operations. Active commits. Python.
author: @0xSteph

title: Anthropic acquires Stainless ($300M)
description: Anthropic acquires Stainless for $300M — the company behind every Anthropic SDK generator and MCP server tool since the early API days
why: Stainless generates the SDKs and MCP tooling that the entire Claude ecosystem depends on. Anthropic now owns the full SDK stack. Combined with the OpenAI+Dell Codex on-prem move the same week, the pattern is clear: model providers are vertically integrating the agent infrastructure layer. The moat is what the agent can safely reach, not just model quality.
author: @AnthropicAI

title: Warp Oz Multi-Agent Orchestration
description: Multi-agent orchestration in Warp's Oz — delegate complex tasks across Claude Code, Codex, and Warp Agent with worktree isolation and message passing
why: 177 likes, 81k views. First terminal-based multi-agent orchestrator that crosses framework boundaries. Each subagent gets its own worktree (local) or Docker container (cloud). The /orchestrate command generates a delegation plan and agents coordinate via structured message passing. This is the 'agent of agents' pattern going mainstream in terminal tools.
author: @warpdotdev

title: Plano
description: AI-native proxy and data plane for agentic apps — LLM routing, safety guardrails, orchestration, and observability in one Rust proxy
why: 6.4k stars, Rust, built on Envoy. The 'Envoy for agents' pattern — sits between your agents and LLM providers handling routing, rate limiting, safety checks, and cost tracking. Most agent teams build this ad-hoc; Plano gives it to you as a drop-in proxy. Solves a real infra gap.
author: @katanemo

title: Cozeloop
description: Full-lifecycle agent optimization platform — dev, debug, eval, and monitor agents from a single Go service
why: 5.4k stars, Go, from ByteDance's Coze team. Agent eval + monitoring + prompt management in one platform. The lifecycle angle matters — most tools do eval OR observability, Cozeloop does both plus a playground for iteration. Good fit for teams running agents in production who need to close the feedback loop between monitoring and improvement.
author: @coze-dev

title: CubeSandbox
description: Hardware-isolated sandbox for AI agents built on RustVMM + KVM — boots in under 60ms, uses less than 5MB per instance
why: From Tencent Cloud. Not containers — actual hardware-level isolation via KVM micro-VMs. E2B SDK compatible. 5.8k stars in 6 weeks, Rust, Apache 2.0. The agent sandbox problem (how do you run untrusted agent code safely?) is one of the unsolved infra gaps. Most solutions use Docker with seccomp. CubeSandbox uses virtualization, which is fundamentally harder to escape. 2000+ concurrent sandboxes on a single node. This is the security layer production agents need.
author: @TencentCloud

title: Open Multi-Agent
description: TypeScript-native multi-agent orchestration — turns a goal into a task DAG automatically, with MCP and live tracing, three runtime dependencies
why: 6.2k stars, MIT, created March 2026. The 3-dependency claim is rare in a space where most frameworks pull in hundreds. Model-agnostic: Claude, Gemini, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama. The goal-to-DAG pattern means you describe what you want, not how agents coordinate. Built-in live tracing solves the visibility gap. TypeScript-native fills the Node.js ecosystem gap that most agent frameworks ignore.
author: @open_multi_agent

title: Sandcastle
description: Orchestrate sandboxed coding agents in TypeScript with sandcastle.run() — single API call spins up an isolated agent on Docker, Podman, or Vercel Firecracker microVMs
why: From Matt Pocock (Total TypeScript). 4.6k stars, MIT, 483 forks. The key insight: agent orchestration needs sandboxing as a first-class concern, not an afterthought. sandcastle.run() handles branch isolation, sandbox provisioning, and merge-back automatically. Provider-agnostic (Docker, Podman, Vercel). This is the 'test runner for agents' pattern — you don't think about the sandbox, you just run. Active commits, 660+ PRs merged.
author: @mattpocock

title: Context Mode
description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents — sandboxes tool output, claims 98% reduction in context usage across 15 platforms
why: 15k stars. #1 on Hacker News (570+ points). Used at Microsoft, Google, Meta per their badges. The real problem: coding agents burn context windows on tool output (npm install logs, file reads, test output). Context Mode intercepts and compresses that output before it hits the model. The 'context budget' problem is one of the main costs in production agents — every wasted token is money. 15 platform integrations (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex, etc). TypeScript.
author: @mksglu

title: DeerFlow
description: Long-horizon SuperAgent by ByteDance — researches, codes, and creates with sandboxes, memories, tools, skills, subagents, and message gateway
why: 68K+ stars. Handles tasks that take minutes to hours with full agent infrastructure — not a demo wrapper. ByteDance-backed and actively maintained.
author: @bytedance

title: OpenSandbox (Alibaba)
description: Secure sandbox runtime for AI agents from Alibaba — extensible plugin architecture for isolation, resource limits, and policy enforcement
why: 10.7k stars, Apache 2.0, Python. The agent sandbox space is consolidating fast: CubeSandbox (Tencent, KVM micro-VMs), OpenSandbox (Alibaba, plugin-based), microsandbox (local Rust), Sandcastle (Matt Pocock, TypeScript). OpenSandbox's angle is extensibility — plugins for custom isolation policies rather than one-size-fits-all containerization. Active commits. Part of the 'agent runtime isolation' infra layer that production agents require.
author: @alibaba

title: microsandbox
description: Secure, local, programmable sandboxes for AI agents — runs entirely on your machine, no cloud dependency, Rust API
why: 6.1k stars, Rust, Apache 2.0. The 'local-first' sandbox. Most agent sandboxes assume cloud infrastructure (E2B, CubeSandbox, Modal). microsandbox targets the dev who wants isolation without shipping execution to someone else's infra. Rust core means small footprint and fast spin-up. The 'run agents locally but safely' pattern matters for teams with data sovereignty constraints or offline requirements.
author: @superradcompany

title: Memori
description: Agent-native memory infrastructure — LLM-agnostic layer that turns agent execution and conversation into structured, persistent state for production systems
why: 14.6k stars, Python, 2200 forks. Different from claude-mem (which is session context persistence). Memori is structured state: it captures execution traces, decisions, and conversation turns, then compresses them into retrievable memory that any LLM can query. The agent-memory problem has two layers — short-term context (solved by bigger windows) and long-term structured recall (still unsolved). Memori targets the second. Production systems need agents that remember what happened across sessions without re-reading the full transcript.
author: @MemoriLabs

title: Engram
description: Persistent memory system for AI coding agents — agent-agnostic Go binary with SQLite + FTS5, MCP server, HTTP API, CLI, and TUI
why: 3.6k stars, MIT, Go. The MCP-native angle matters: instead of a standalone memory service, Engram exposes memory through the same MCP interface coding agents already use. SQLite + FTS5 means zero external dependencies — no vector DB, no Redis. The Go binary is a single deployable unit. For teams running Claude Code or Codex, adding persistent memory becomes one MCP server config instead of infrastructure. The lightweight approach (SQLite vs vector DB) is the right tradeoff for coding agent memory — you need exact recall of past decisions, not semantic similarity.
author: @GentlemanProg

title: CUA (Computer Use Agents)
description: Open-source infrastructure for Computer-Use Agents — sandboxes, SDKs, and benchmarks for agents that control full desktops across macOS, Linux, and Windows
why: 16.9k stars, MIT, 1069 forks. The first cross-platform Computer Use Agent stack. While browser-use agents dominate, CUA goes further: full desktop control (not just browser) across all 3 OSes. Ships sandboxes, SDKs, and eval benchmarks together. Active commits (last push today). The computer-use pattern is moving from browser-only to full desktop — CUA owns that layer. 307 open issues shows real community engagement, not a trophy repo.
author: @trycua

title: memU
description: Memory system built for 24/7 proactive agents like OpenClaw — persistent, structured memory that survives across agent sessions and restarts
why: 13.6k stars, 1028 forks. Purpose-built for always-on agents. Most agent memory solutions target chatbots (session context). memU targets the harder problem: agents that run 24/7 need to accumulate state, learn from past runs, and maintain consistency across restarts. Explicitly designed for OpenClaw-compatible proactive agents. Python. The proactive-agent memory layer is underserved — Memori and Engram focus on coding agents, memU focuses on background agents that never stop.
author: @NevaMindAI

title: ZeroLang
description: Agent-first programming language from Vercel Labs — designed for AI agents as primary users, with structured diagnostics, tiny static binaries, and learnable syntax
why: 3.4k stars in 5 days. The core idea: programming languages have been optimized for human readability for 50 years. What happens when the primary consumer is an AI agent? Zero explores this — structured JSON diagnostics agents can parse, error repair codes, sub-16KB static builds, explicit capabilities. Written in C, Apache 2.0. Pre-1.0 and intentionally unstable, but the concept is a genuine shift in thinking about the agent-tooling interface.
author: @vercel

title: audit (evilsocket)
description: 8-stage vulnerability discovery agent — reimplements Cloudflare's Project Glasswing pipeline with narrow agents, deliberate disagreement, and reachability tracing
why: 308 stars, 2 days old, MIT. From evilsocket (bettercap creator). The architecture matters: instead of one big 'find bugs' prompt, it runs 8 narrow stages — recon, hunt, validate (adversarial — tries to disprove), gapfill, dedupe, reachability trace, feedback loop, report. Uses Opus 4.7 for critical stages, Sonnet 4.6 for high-volume ones. The reachability gate is the key insight: most findings are noise unless attacker input can reach the sink. Built on Claude Code Agent SDK, uses subscription billing. Real security tooling, not a demo.
author: @evilsocket

title: agentmemory
description: Persistent memory for AI coding agents — extends Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern with confidence scoring, lifecycle, knowledge graphs, and hybrid search
why: 14.3k stars, TypeScript, Apache 2.0. MCP-native — works with Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, OpenClaw out of the box. The Karpathy LLM Wiki design doc got 1200 stars on its own before this implementation shipped. Uses the iii engine under the hood. Confidence scoring on memories (not just store-and-retrieve) means agents can weigh how much to trust recalled context. This is the memory layer coding agents actually need — persistent across sessions, queryable via MCP, no vector DB required.
author: @rohitg00

title: τ³-bench (tau-three-bench)
description: Multimodal benchmark for agent evaluation — now covers text, voice (full-duplex), and knowledge retrieval domains with a live leaderboard
why: 1206 stars, MIT, from Sierra. The τ-bench series is becoming the standard for agent evaluation beyond coding tasks. τ³ adds voice evaluation with realtime providers (OpenAI, Gemini, xAI) and a knowledge domain with configurable RAG pipelines. Live leaderboard at taubench.com. 75+ task quality fixes based on SABER analysis. Most agent benchmarks test code generation. τ-bench tests the full tool-agent-user interaction loop in real domains (airline, retail, banking). The voice evaluation layer is new — nobody else is benchmarking full-duplex voice agents systematically.
author: @SierraPlatform

title: LiteLLM Agent Platform
description: Self-hosted platform for running coding agents in isolated sandboxes with a credential vault — agents get stub keys, vault swaps them for real ones on every outbound TLS call
why: 438 stars, MIT, TypeScript, from the LiteLLM team. The vault proxy is the key insight: agents run with bypass-permissions but never see real credentials. Supports Claude Code, Codex, and Hermes out of the box. Uses Kubernetes agent-sandbox CRDs. Most agent sandboxing solutions handle isolation; this one handles the harder problem of credential management inside the sandbox. BerriAI already owns the LLM proxy layer (20k+ stars on LiteLLM), so extending to agent infra is a natural move with existing distribution.
author: @BerriAI

title: Raindrop Workshop
description: Local debugger for AI agents that streams every token, tool call, and decision in realtime — then lets Claude Code read your traces, write evals, and fix what's broken
why: 674 stars in 19 days, TypeScript. The self-healing eval loop is the key insight: your coding agent reads its own traces, writes assertions against past failures, fixes the code, and re-runs until everything passes. Compatible with every major SDK (Vercel AI, OpenAI Agents, Anthropic, LangChain, etc). Local-first with SQLite storage. This is the 'test-driven development for agents' pattern — instead of humans writing evals, the agent reads its failure traces and generates them. 8 releases in 3 weeks shows shipping velocity.
author: @raindrop_ai

title: SmallCode
description: Terminal-native coding agent built for small local models (7B-20B) — compensates for small model limitations with budget-managed context, forgiving tool-call parsing, TODO-file decomposed planning, and search-and-replace patches instead of full file rewrites
why: 746 stars in 2 days, MIT, JavaScript. 87% benchmark with 4B-active model. Most coding agents assume frontier models with 128k+ context. SmallCode targets the opposite end: consumer hardware running Ollama or LM Studio. RTK (Rust Token Killer) integration rewrites bash commands for 60-90% token savings. Budget-managed context instead of dumping everything. Forgiven multi-format tool call parser instead of assuming reliable JSON. TODO-file decomposed planning instead of single-shot. Already at v0.6.14 with active PRs. Works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This matters because not every team can or should send every line of code to a frontier model API — privacy, cost, latency, sovereignty all push toward local agents that actually work.
author: @Doorman11991

title: OneCLI
description: Open-source credential vault for AI agents — agents access services without ever seeing real keys, MCP-compatible
why: 2.2k stars, TypeScript + Rust, Apache 2.0. The credential management problem is agent infra's biggest unsolved gap. Most teams put API keys in env vars and hope. OneCLI intercepts at the tool layer — agents get short-lived session tokens, never raw secrets. MCP-compatible, works with OpenClaw and Hermes. Topics include secret-management, security, vault. Complements LiteLLM's vault proxy approach (TLS interception) with a CLI-first vault model (token vending). The space is converging: CubeSandbox for isolation, LiteLLM for TLS proxy creds, OneCLI for CLI-level credential vending. 33 open issues, active development.
author: @onecli

title: NanoClaw
description: Lightweight container-first alternative to OpenClaw — runs agents in isolated containers with built-in memory, scheduled jobs, and connects to WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Gmail
why: 29K stars, MIT, TypeScript, 4 months old. The container-first approach means every agent gets its own sandbox by default — no extra config. Runs on Anthropic Agents SDK directly, not another abstraction layer. Connects to 6+ messaging platforms out of the box. The market needed an OpenClaw alternative that takes security seriously from the architecture level rather than bolting it on. 12.8K forks shows massive community contribution velocity.
author: @nanocoai

title: IronClaw
description: Agent OS built in Rust focused on privacy, security, and extensibility — uses WebAssembly for sandboxed agent plugins
why: 12.3K stars, Apache 2.0, Rust. Near AI built this with a privacy-first architecture: agents run in WASM sandboxes with explicit permission boundaries. The Rust choice isn't aesthetic — memory safety in an agent runtime that handles credentials and tool execution matters. CodeAct + RLM patterns built in. The WASM plugin model means third-party agent extensions can't escape their sandbox. This is the 'secure by default' approach that most agent frameworks skip.
author: @nearai

title: MCP-Universe
description: RL training and benchmarking framework for MCP tool-use agents — lets you train agents to use tools via reinforcement learning and evaluate them on standardized benchmarks
why: 587 stars, Apache 2.0, Python, from Salesforce AI Research. Most MCP work is hand-wired: you connect servers, test manually, hope it works. MCP-Universe treats tool-use as an RL problem — agents learn which tools to call, when, and with what parameters through reward signals. Includes benchmarking environments to compare agent strategies. This bridges the gap between 'MCP server exists' and 'agent actually uses MCP tools well.' 82 forks, actively maintained.
author: @SalesforceAI

title: Varlock
description: AI-safe .env files — separates schema definitions (safe for agents to read) from secret values (only humans access), preventing agents from ever seeing raw credentials in config files
why: 3.4K stars, MIT, TypeScript. The problem is real: every coding agent reads .env files and gets access to every secret. Varlock splits config into schema (what keys exist, their types, validation rules) and secrets (actual values). Agents get the schema to understand the configuration surface without ever touching the values. Simple idea, clean execution, solves the root cause of most agent credential leaks. 90 forks, active development since April 2025.
author: @dmno_dev

title: DeepAgents
description: Batteries-included agent harness from LangChain — planning, sub-agents, filesystem, context management, persistent memory, skills, and MCP tool support built on LangGraph
why: 23K stars, MIT, Python + TypeScript. LangChain built this as the opinionated layer above LangGraph — the same graph runtime, but with all the pieces a production agent needs: sub-agents with isolated context, filesystem operations (local/sandboxed/remote), context summarization for long threads, shell access, persistent memory, human-in-the-loop, and a skills system. Model-agnostic — works with any LLM that supports tool calling. The 'Deep Agents Code' CLI is their answer to Claude Code, powered by any model. 160 open issues shows active community. Important because it codifies the pattern most teams build ad-hoc: agent + filesystem + memory + eval + deployment as a single package.
author: @langchain_oss

title: Eval Engineer
description: Open-source skill bundle that turns Claude Code and Codex into eval engineers backed by Galileo traces — inspect, diagnose, fix, and verify agent behavior through evidence
why: MIT, Python, from Galileo Agent Labs. This is the eval loop most agent teams are missing. Install into a project and Claude Code gets /eval-engineer, /eval-diagnose, /eval-cost, /eval-audit as slash commands. Codex gets the same as $mentions. The flow: fetch Galileo traces, build a debug packet, run RCA on spans and metrics, make one bounded change, verify the next run improved. It's not a dashboard — it's an agent skill that knows which artifact to inspect, which metric matters, and whether the fix belongs in the prompt, tool schema, retriever, or config. Directly useful for Hermes and any agent running eval cycles.
author: @rungalileo

title: Infisical Agent Vault
description: HTTP credential proxy and vault for AI agents — intercepts outbound requests and injects real credentials so agents never see raw secrets
why: 1232 stars, Go, from Infisical (established secrets management platform). The proxy pattern is different from OneCLI (CLI-level token vending) and LiteLLM (TLS proxy for sandbox pods). Agent Vault sits at the HTTP layer: any agent that makes outbound API calls gets credentials injected transparently. Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Hermes, and custom agents. 11 open issues, pushed today (active development). The credential management space for agents is converging on three approaches: CLI vending (OneCLI), TLS proxy (LiteLLM), and HTTP proxy (Agent Vault). Teams running multiple agent types need one of these — env vars don't cut it.
author: @Infisical

title: Obsidian Mind
description: Obsidian vault that gives AI coding agents persistent memory — works with Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI out of the box
why: 2592 stars, MIT, TypeScript, 327 forks. The Obsidian angle is clever: instead of building a custom memory UI, it uses Obsidian's graph view, backlinks, and search as the memory interface for coding agents. Agents write structured markdown notes; humans browse and edit the same vault. The bidirectional flow matters — agents accumulate knowledge during coding sessions, humans can curate and correct it in Obsidian, and agents read back the corrections. 327 forks shows community customization. Created Feb 2026, active through May. Works with the three major coding CLIs. Part of the 'memory as filesystem' pattern (like agentmemory's iii engine) but with a polished UI layer.
author: @breferrari

title: Laminar
description: Open-source observability platform purpose-built for AI agents — traces, evals, monitoring, SQL access to all data, written in Rust
why: 2917 stars, Apache 2.0, YC S24, TypeScript + Rust. OpenTelemetry-native: 1 line of code to trace Vercel AI SDK, LangChain, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Browser Use. The Rust core means it handles high-throughput agent traces without buckling. Self-hostable via Docker compose. The SQL access to traces matters — most agent observability tools give you dashboards but no way to query the raw data. Laminar gives you both. gRPC exporter for pipeline integration. Compared to Langfuse (also open-source agent observability), Laminar is Rust-native and OpenTelemetry-first, while Langfuse is Python-based. The monitoring layer uses natural language event definitions to detect issues — not just metric thresholds.
author: @lmnrai

title: ClawBench
description: Open-source benchmark for browser AI agents — 153 everyday tasks across 144 live websites with 5-layer recording, DOM-match, and LLM judge
why: 310 stars, Apache 2.0, Python. Published as arXiv paper (2604.08523), featured as HuggingFace Daily Paper. The top score is 33.3% — which means the best browser agents fail on 2/3 of everyday web tasks. 144 live websites, not sandboxed mock environments. 5-layer recording (screenshot, DOM, network, console, accessibility tree) gives evaluators rich failure data. DOM-match + LLM judge for scoring. Has a published dataset on HuggingFace. Most agent benchmarks test coding or tool use; ClawBench tests the thing users actually want agents to do: navigate real websites and complete multi-step tasks. The low top score tells you the field needs this benchmark.
author: @reacher_z

title: TencentDB Agent Memory
description: 4-tier progressive memory pipeline for AI agents — symbolic short-term memory (Mermaid symbol offloading) + layered long-term memory (L0 raw → L1 facts → L2 summaries → L3 personas), fully local, zero external dependencies
why: 3618 stars, MIT, TypeScript. From Tencent. The benchmarks are concrete: 61.38% token reduction on WideSearch, +51.52% pass rate, PersonaMem accuracy 48%→76%. The 4-layer architecture matters — L0 raw conversations, L1 atomic facts, L2 structured summaries, L3 user personas. Symbolic short-term memory compresses tool logs into Mermaid diagrams instead of raw text. Zero external deps (no Redis, no vector DB) — runs fully local. OpenClaw plugin, Hermes compatible. 287 forks, pushed today. The memory layer is where agent infra is converging: Memori (structured state), Engram (MCP-native SQLite), agentmemory (confidence scoring), and now TencentDB (4-tier pipeline with real benchmarks). Each solves a different slice. TencentDB's contribution is the progressive compression pipeline with measured impact.
author: @Tencent

title: Beads
description: Distributed graph issue tracker for AI coding agents — replaces markdown TODO lists with a Dolt-backed SQL database, dependency chains, memory compaction, and zero-conflict multi-agent coordination
why: 23.9K stars, MIT, Go. From Steve Yegge. The core idea: agents lose context because markdown plans aren't queryable, don't update as agents work, and bit-rot within hours. Beads replaces that with a version-controlled SQL database (Dolt) where every issue is a row, dependencies are queryable graph edges, and old tasks get semantically compacted to save context window. Hash-based IDs prevent merge collisions when multiple agents work the same codebase. Integrations for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, Factory. Stealth mode for personal use on shared repos. Compaction feature summarizes old closed tasks — essentially memory decay for the issue tracker. 1582 forks shows real adoption. Active development with daily commits.
author: @gastownhall

title: Agent Governance Toolkit
description: Runtime governance for AI agents — every tool call, resource access, and inter-agent message evaluated against policy before execution, deterministic, sub-millisecond, auditable
why: 1596 stars, MIT, Python/TS/.NET/Rust/Go, from Microsoft. The benchmark data is the key differentiator: prompt-based safety has 26.67% policy violation rate in red-team testing; this does 0.00% by evaluating at the application layer before execution. Covers all 10 OWASP Agentic Top 10. Multi-language SDKs (PyPI, npm, NuGet). Works with LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, OpenAI Agents, Google ADK, Semantic Kernel, AWS Bedrock, and 20+ more frameworks. Policy as code — define rules declaratively, evaluate before every action. The architecture is a PolicyEvaluator that runs before each tool call: Agent Action → Policy Check → Allow/Deny → Audit Log in < 0.1ms. 308 forks, pushed today. Part of the governance/safety layer that production agents need — complements observability (Laminar) and memory (TencentDB) in the agent infra stack. OpenSSF Scorecard and Best Practices certified.
author: @microsoft

title: Forge (antoinezambelli)
description: Reliability layer for self-hosted LLM tool-calling — lifts 8B local models to 86.5% on multi-step agentic evals through rescue parsing, retry nudges, step enforcement, and VRAM-aware context budgets
why: 952 stars, MIT, Python. The core problem: small local models (8B) fail at agentic workflows because they hallucinate tool calls, skip steps, or blow their context window. Forge fixes all three. Rescue parsing catches malformed tool calls and re-prompts. Step enforcement makes sure the agent actually does each step. VRAM-aware budgets compact context before OOM. Three usage modes: WorkflowRunner (full agent loop), guardrails middleware (plug into your own loop), or proxy server (drop-in between any client and local model). The eval suite has 26 scenarios across 3 tiers. Top config: Ministral-3 8B Q8 scores 86.5%. The ablation study (N=50) shows each guardrail contributes measurably. Works with Ollama, llama-server, Llamafile, and Anthropic. This is the infrastructure layer teams need when they can't or won't send everything to frontier APIs — and unlike most 'local agent' projects, it measures its claims.
author: @antoinezambelli

title: MCPMark
description: Stress-testing benchmark for MCP tool-use — evaluates agents across real MCP servers (Notion, GitHub, Filesystem, Postgres, Playwright) with isolated sandboxes and unified metrics
why: 419 stars, Apache 2.0, Python. Has an arXiv paper (2509.24002) and HuggingFace trajectory dataset. DeepSeek v3.2 used MCPMark in their evaluation — the best open-source model picked it as their MCP benchmark. Pinned MCP server versions for reproducibility. Auto-compaction support to avoid context overflow during long evaluations. 50 easy tasks for smaller open-source models plus harder tasks for frontier models. The leaderboard tells the story: gpt-5-high scores 51.6%, gemini-3-pro 50.6%, deepseek-v3.2-thinking 36.8%. Most agents fail on half the MCP tasks — which means the benchmark is measuring real capability, not participation trophies. Complements MCP-Universe (RL training for MCP) in the evaluation stack.
author: @eval_sys

title: OpenViking
description: Context database for AI agents — unifies memory, resources, and skills under a filesystem paradigm with tiered loading (L0/L1/L2) and observable retrieval trajectories
why: 24.2K stars, AGPL, Python, from ByteDance/Volcengine. The filesystem paradigm is different from TencentDB (4-tier progressive compression) and Memori (structured state): OpenViking treats context as a hierarchical filesystem where memories, resources, and skills are files and directories. L0/L1/L2 tiered loading loads context on demand instead of dumping everything into the context window. Directory recursive retrieval combines directory positioning with semantic search for precise context retrieval. Visualized retrieval trajectories make context fetching observable — you can see why the agent fetched what it fetched. Auto session management compresses conversations and extracts long-term memory. Rust CLI + Python package. 1815 forks, active since Jan 2026 with frequent releases. The retrieval observability angle matters: most agent context systems are black boxes. OpenViking makes the retrieval chain visible and debuggable.
author: @volcengine

title: Chrome DevTools MCP
description: Chrome DevTools as MCP server — lets coding agents control and inspect a live browser for debugging, performance, and automation
why: First-class browser debugging for AI agents. Performance traces, network requests, source-mapped console errors — all through MCP. Google-backed, 40K stars.
author: @ChromeDevTools

title: Ruflo
description: Agent orchestration platform for Claude — deploy multi-agent swarms with self-learning coordination, RAG, and native Claude Code/Codex integration
why: De facto standard for orchestrating multiple Claude Code instances. 53K stars, 22M+ npm downloads, swarm intelligence with memory persistence. Formerly claude-flow.
author: @ruvnet

title: ECC
description: Harness-native operator system for coding agents — skills, instincts, memory optimization, security scanning, and research-first development across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, and 7+ other agent harnesses
why: 187K stars, MIT, JavaScript + TypeScript + Python + Go. Anthropic hackathon winner. 170+ contributors, 12+ language ecosystems. Not just configs — a complete system: skills (reusable agent capabilities), instincts (automatic behavior patterns), memory optimization (context budget management), security scanning (agent output validation), and research-first development (agents search before coding). Cross-harness: same skills work in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Zed, GitHub Copilot. The v2.0.0-rc.1 adds a publish/subscribe system for inter-agent communication. 29K forks, active daily development. This matters because most coding agent setups are single-tool (Claude Code config OR Cursor rules OR Codex instructions). ECC treats the agent harness as a platform and builds a portable skill/memory layer on top of it.
author: @affaan_m

title: Acontext
description: Agent skills as a memory layer — captures learnings from agent runs as plain markdown files, no embeddings, no API lock-in, git-friendly
why: 3.3K stars, Apache 2.0, JavaScript. The 'Skill is Memory' concept is different from every other memory project: instead of vector DBs, embeddings, or compression pipelines, Acontext stores agent learnings as markdown skill files. You can read them, edit them, version them with git, share them across agents and frameworks. No opaque memory polluting context — everything is inspectable. Works with LangGraph, Claude, AI SDK, and anything that reads files. The philosophy is that if skills can represent all knowledge an agent needs, then memory can too. Self-evolving skills that grow from agent mistakes and successes. 315 forks, 33 open issues. Complements claude-mem (session context), Memori (structured state), and TencentDB (progressive compression) by solving memory from the skill-file angle.
author: @memodb_io

title: ExploitBench
description: Progressive difficulty benchmark that measures how far AI agents climb from finding vulnerable code to building working exploits — code analysis → trigger → primitive → RCE
why: 157 stars, MIT, Python, 6 days old. Most agent benchmarks measure if code works. ExploitBench measures if agents can break things — and how far they get. Uses V8 as first target (16 capabilities in the Chromium V8 exploitation ladder). Drives containers through an MCP server so any LLM can run evaluations. Has a leaderboard at exploitbench.ai. The exploit ladder concept matters: instead of a binary pass/fail, it measures progressive capability. An agent that finds the bug but can't trigger it scores differently from one that reaches RCE. Pre-built V8 eval images on GHCR (~70 GB each, no local build needed). Works with direct provider APIs or OpenAI-compatible gateways. 9 forks, 3 open issues, active development. This fills a gap in the agent eval space: Tau³-bench measures reliability, ClawBench measures coding accuracy, but nothing measured the full security exploit chain until now.
author: @exploitbench
